title: Does failed development work count for R&D tax credits?
description: Failed or abandoned development work can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit for US taxpayers.
summary: Failed or abandoned development work can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit for US taxpayers. Under IRC §41 and Treasury regulations, eligibility depends on whether the work sought to resolve a genuine technological uncertainty through a systematic process of experimentation, not on success. Work stopped for technical reasons can qualify; budget- or market-driven stops generally do not.

body.text: Failed or abandoned development work can qualify for the federal R&D tax credit for US taxpayers. Under IRC §41 and Treasury regulations, eligibility depends on whether the work sought to resolve a genuine technological uncertainty through a systematic process of experimentation, not on success. Work stopped for technical reasons can qualify; budget- or market-driven stops generally do not.
This report is informational and is not legal or tax advice.
Summary

Yes, failed or abandoned development work can count. In the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, eligibility turns on whether the work tried to resolve a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty through a systematic process, not on whether the intended result was achieved. The law in each jurisdiction says this in its own words, and each version is identified below. For a US taxpayer, the controlling texts are Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §41 and the Treasury regulations that interpret it, read together with the research and experimental expenditure rules that §41(d)(1)(A) now ties to section 174A.

Two qualifications matter as much as the headline answer. First, failure does not by itself prove that a project qualified: the claimant still has to show the uncertainty, the alternatives considered and how they were evaluated. Second, the reason for stopping matters. Work stopped because of a technical barrier can qualify; work stopped for budget or market reasons generally does not, though qualifying work done before the stop may still be claimable.
The legal rule in each jurisdiction
United States: success is not required

The Treasury regulations state the rule directly. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), a determination that research is undertaken for the purpose of discovering technological information does not require the taxpayer to succeed in developing a new or improved business component. Under Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1), whether costs qualify as research or experimental expenditures depends on the nature of the activity to which the costs relate, not the nature of the product or improvement being developed or the level of technological advancement it represents, and the ultimate success, failure, sale or use of the product is not relevant to that determination.

The statute (IRC §41) does not contain that statement; it appears in the Treasury regulations cited above, which interpret the statute. The distinction matters in an examination or in litigation, because a taxpayer relying on the rule should cite the regulation by section and paragraph rather than the Code.

Update on the statutory cross-reference: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) added section 174A, which restores current deduction of domestic research or experimental expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, and amended §41(d)(1)(A) so that the first prong of the qualified research definition now refers to expenditures treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A. The regulatory definition of research or experimental expenditures in Treas. Reg. §1.174-2, including its statement that success or failure is irrelevant, remains the principal regulatory text on what counts as research for this purpose.
United Kingdom: the DSIT Guidelines

For accounting periods beginning after March 31, 2023, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) Guidelines on the Meaning of Research and Development for Tax Purposes have legal force through SI 2023/293 and are reproduced in HMRC's manual at CIRD81910. Three paragraphs bear on failed work:

items: Paragraph 10: even if the advance in science or technology sought by a project is not achieved or not fully realized, R&D still takes place.

Paragraph 13 defines scientific or technological uncertainty as existing where knowledge of whether something is scientifically possible or technologically feasible, or how to achieve it in practice, is not readily available or deducible by a competent professional working in the field. Paragraph 14 excludes uncertainties that such a professional could readily resolve.
Paragraph 38, on abortive projects, treats scientific or technological planning activities for projects that are not taken forward as R&D.

body.text: It is in the DSIT Guidelines themselves (paragraph 38), which HMRC's CIRD manual reproduces.
Canada: SR&ED

The Canada Revenue Agency's guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives (last modified July 5, 2022) state that success or failure in meeting objectives is not relevant when assessing the "Why" requirement. The same guidance defines scientific or technological uncertainty as arising when it is unknown whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, because the available knowledge or experience is insufficient.
Australia: the R&D Tax Incentive

Under section 355-25(1) of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997, core R&D activities are experimental activities whose outcome cannot be known or determined in advance on the basis of current knowledge, information or experience, and can only be determined by applying a systematic progression of work. The government's program guidance at business.gov.au explains that a competent professional in the field must be unable to know or determine the outcome in advance from knowledge available anywhere in the world, without conducting the experiment.
The OECD Frascati Manual

The Frascati Manual (7th edition, 2015) sets five criteria for an R&D activity: novel, creative, uncertain, systematic, and transferable and/or reproducible. "Uncertain" covers uncertainty about the final outcome, including the time and resources needed to achieve it, which supports the idea that unsuccessful work can still be R&D.

Qualification (analysis): the Frascati Manual is a methodology for collecting and reporting R&D statistics. Its own text says that chapter's definitions are for measurement purposes. Tax eligibility is set by each country's legislation: IRC §41 and its regulations in the US, and in the UK the GAAP-based definition in ITA 2007 s.1006 as modified by the DSIT Guidelines. The four regimes share a focus on uncertainty and systematic work, but "rooted in Frascati" overstates the legal link, particularly for the United States, where neither the Code nor the regulations incorporate the Frascati criteria and courts apply the statutory four-part test.
Applying the US four-part test to failed work
IRC §41(d) defines qualified research. The tests are commonly summarized as four parts. The table below states each test as the statute and regulations frame it and how failed work interacts with it.

headers: How it applies to failed work (analysis)

cells: §41(d)(1)(A): the expenditures must be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A (before the 2025 amendment, the reference was to specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174). Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1) says uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product.
Uncertainty is judged at the outset. A later failure is consistent with uncertainty having existed, but the claimant must still show what was unknown at the start.

§41(d)(1)(B)(i): the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover it fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.
The disciplines used in the attempt determine this test, not the outcome.

§41(d)(1)(B)(ii): the application of the information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) states that success in developing the component is not required.
The intended component, as shown in project briefs and objectives, satisfies this even if it was never completed.

§41(d)(1)(C): substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose listed in §41(d)(3), which covers a new or improved function, performance, reliability or quality. Research related to style, taste, cosmetic or seasonal design factors is excluded. Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(5)(i) describes the process as one designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain at the outset. Under Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(a)(6), "substantially all" means 80 percent or more of the research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis.
Records of hypotheses, tests and results before abandonment carry this test. Failed test results are part of the evidence.

body.text: §41(d)(4) also lists exclusions that apply regardless of outcome, including research after the beginning of commercial production, adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement, duplication of an existing business component, surveys, studies and efficiency surveys, management functions and market research, routine data collection and routine quality control testing, research conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico or a US possession, research in the social sciences, arts or humanities, and research funded by any grant, contract or otherwise by another person or governmental entity.
Does failure prove uncertainty?

It states that failure alone does not establish that a project qualified, and that the company must still show the technical uncertainty, the alternatives it considered and how it evaluated them. If the capability, method or design was already known at the start, the uncertainty requirement is not met.

The regulatory text supports KBKG's position. Under the UK Guidelines (paragraph 14), an uncertainty that a competent professional could readily resolve is not a scientific or technological uncertainty, whether or not a particular team managed to resolve it. Under Treas. Reg. §1.174-2(a)(1), uncertainty is measured against the information available to the taxpayer at the outset. A project can fail because of poor execution of known methods, and that failure is not evidence of qualifying uncertainty.

Analysis: Failure is consistent with genuine uncertainty and can be good evidence of it when contemporaneous records show the team tried reasonable alternatives that a competent professional would also have tried. It is not proof on its own. For a US claim, the stronger evidence is a record, made at the start of the work, of what the team did not know about capability, method or design, followed by records of each alternative evaluated and why it was rejected.
Technical abandonment versus commercial abandonment
All four regimes look for uncertainty that is scientific or technological rather than commercial.

items: KBKG gives examples of technical stops that can qualify: a prototype that misses required performance tolerances, or a software team that cannot reduce latency below a critical threshold despite several development sprints. Stops for budget shifts, changing market conditions or weak customer interest generally do not qualify.
In Australia, market research, market testing and sales promotion cannot be core R&D activities (business.gov.au).
Under §41(d)(4)(D), efficiency surveys, management functions and market research are excluded from qualified research.

body.text: The Leyton article does list "the technology would be too expensive to develop" as an example of a failed R&D project, but it does not discuss costs up to the point of abandonment. It says only that a claim requires qualifying activity before the project ended. Analysis: the principle that follows from the rules above is that the reason for stopping does not decide eligibility for work already done. Work done before a commercial decision to stop can qualify if that work itself met the tests. What a commercial stop does not supply is evidence that a technical uncertainty existed.
Which costs can be claimed on a failed project

The cost rules for failed projects are the same as for successful ones. Leyton puts it plainly for the UK: the rules for claiming are exactly the same for failed or abortive projects as for successful ones. In the US, nothing in §41(b) makes the inclusion of wages, supplies or contract research depend on the outcome of the research.

cells: Wages for qualified services: engaging in qualified research, or the direct supervision or direct support of research activities that constitute qualified research (§41(b)(2)(B)).

Supplies used in the conduct of qualified research. "Supplies" means tangible property other than land, improvements to land and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (§41(b)(2)(C)).
65% of amounts paid or incurred to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for qualified research (§41(b)(3)(A)).

Contracted-out R&D and externally provided workers; payments to unconnected parties are generally included at 65%, with restrictions on overseas work for periods beginning on or after April 1, 2024 (HMRC CIRD138000; commentary from Saffery).
Amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research, to the extent provided by regulations (§41(b)(2)(A)(iii)).
Software, and for accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2023, data licenses and cloud computing services (GOV.UK).

body.text: That is right for the UK. In the US, software licenses are not in the statutory list: supplies must be tangible property, and the computing category covers payments for the right to use computers.

For context (analysis), the US credit is not a flat percentage of qualified research expenses: under §41(a)(1) the regular credit is 20% of qualified research expenses above a base amount, and under §41(c)(4) the alternative simplified credit is 14% of qualified research expenses above 50% of the average for the three preceding tax years (6% if there were no qualified research expenses in any one of those years), with the effective rate further affected by the §280C(c) election.
Hypothetical example: US qualified research expenses on an abandoned project
This example is hypothetical. It computes qualified research expenses only, not the credit, because the credit depends on the method and base amount chosen.
A company spends the following on a sensor-calibration project that it abandons after testing shows the target accuracy cannot be reached with the available hardware:

cells: Wages for engineers doing and directly supervising the testing
Outside testing lab doing qualified research for the company

body.text: Check: $50,000 × 0.65 = $32,500. $150,000 + $32,500 + $10,000 = $192,500. $150,000 + $50,000 + $10,000 = $210,000. All of this assumes the project passed every part of §41(d), which the abandonment itself does not establish. It also assumes that the company's payments to the outside lab were not contingent on the success of the research and that the company retains substantial rights in the results, as Treas. Reg. §1.41-2(e)(2) requires for contract research expenses. This condition is directly relevant to failed work: if the lab would have been paid only if the research succeeded, the lab, not the company, bore the risk of failure, and the company could not include the payment.
Documentation for failed projects
United States

Treas. Reg. §1.41-4(d) requires a taxpayer claiming the credit to retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. For a failed project, this means the records have to show qualifying activity even though no finished business component exists to point to.

Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) was revised for the 2024 tax year. Section G, which collects business component information, has been optional for tax years beginning before 2026. In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS said Section G would be optional for all filers for tax year 2025 and mandatory from tax year 2026, with optional reporting for some filers, including qualified small business taxpayers electing the reduced payroll tax credit. The IRS then released final Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) on or about February 5 to 6, 2026, which state that Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 and required for tax years beginning after 2025, subject to the exceptions set out under "Requirements To Complete Section G." As of this report, the final instructions are in force, the January 2025 revision of the form is required for 2025 returns, and tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026 require Section G for most filers. For a failed project, Section G reporting means the abandoned business component, its information sought and its share of qualified research expenses will be disclosed component by component on the return.

For refund claims, The Tax Adviser (October 2025) reports that the IRS's 2021 requirements for research credit refund claims originally called for five items, and that a June 2024 update waived two of them at filing (the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each sought to discover), leaving business components, research activities and total qualified employee wage, supply and contract research expenses required. IR-2025-99 also extended the transition period during which taxpayers have 45 days to perfect a research credit refund claim that the IRS finds lacking, through January 10, 2027.

The case is Jeffrey A. Harper et ux. v. United States, No. 19-55933 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021), 847 Fed. App'x 408, an unpublished memorandum disposition. The Ninth Circuit reversed a dismissal and held that the IRS, through a four-year audit directed at the taxpayer's research credit, had waived the specificity requirement in 26 C.F.R. §301.6402-2(b)(1). It was a taxpayer win on a procedural point. It did not impose new documentation requirements, although refund-claim specificity has drawn more attention since.
Australia

In Australia, the business.gov.au guidance asks claimants to keep records showing how they determined the outcome was unknown, and records of each step of the systematic progression of work: hypothesis, experiment, observation, evaluation and logical conclusions. Examples it gives include records of trial runs and test reports with results and analysis.
What the records should show for an abandoned project

KBKG recommends keeping design trials, testing notes, lab results, revision logs, development tickets, meeting notes, closeout materials, final test results, team debriefs and the benchmarks that were not met, and linking each business component to the employees, tests and expenses claimed while the work is recent. Analysis: these are recommendations from advisers rather than statutory requirements, but each one maps to a test above: the starting uncertainty, the alternatives evaluated, and the technical reason for stopping. Because Section G now asks for information at the business component level, an abandonment report that names the component, the information sought and the reason the work stopped also supplies the facts a US filer will need to complete the form for tax years beginning after 2025.
Conclusion

Failed development work can count for R&D tax credits in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, and the official texts say so. In the United States, Treas. Reg. §§1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and 1.174-2(a)(1) make success irrelevant to eligibility, while IRC §41(d) still requires the work to meet each part of the qualified research test. What decides a failed project's claim is whether the work, judged at the time, faced a genuine technical uncertainty and was carried out systematically, and whether records made at the time show that. For US filers, those records now also feed component-level reporting on Form 6765 Section G for tax years beginning after 2025.
